name: Beef tallow
lead: Beef tallow is rendered beef fat, a solid at room temperature made mostly of triglycerides. In looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet circles it is used in two ways to improve appearance: as a cooking fat in place of seed oils, with the aim of a leaner physique and clearer skin through diet, and as a face and body moisturiser applied directly to skin, where proponents say it softens and smooths [1].

Beef tallow is about 50 percent saturated fat, 42 percent monounsaturated and 4 percent polyunsaturated, with roughly 109 mg of cholesterol per 100 g and about 902 kcal per 100 g [1]. It has a smoke point of about 249 C (480 F), which is why it was traditionally used for deep frying; McDonald's cooked its fries in a beef tallow and cottonseed oil blend until 1990 [1][9]. It has also long served as the raw material for soap, candles and lubricants [1].

In the 2020s tallow became a social-media and political trend. It is promoted within the seed-oil-avoidance and Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movements, and in 2025 the restaurant chain Steak 'n Shake announced fries cooked in 100 percent beef tallow, a change praised by US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and criticised by some health experts [10][11]. Alongside the diet trend, tallow-based balms became a popular skincare product, and a 2025 cross-sectional analysis in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined how tallow skincare claims are presented on social media [5].

Nutrition organisations and Wikipedia describe the claims that tallow is a healthier frying fat than seed oils as unsupported by the scientific literature, and cardiology reviews link beef tallow with higher LDL cholesterol [1][3][8]; supporters of the practice answer that animal fats are traditional foods and that industrial seed oils are the concern. No published human trial has tested tallow, eaten or applied, for skin condition or appearance.

angle.text: Users rub tallow-based balms on the face and body as a moisturiser, saying the fat resembles skin oils and leaves skin supple. Moisturisers in general work partly by sealing in water [4], but tallow itself has not been tested for skin outcomes. Dietary tallow is used as a seed-oil-free cooking fat.

paras: In industry, tallow refers to animal fat that meets technical criteria such as melting point, not only rendered suet from beef or mutton. In Britain rendered beef fat is called dripping. The main fatty acids are palmitic (about 25 percent), stearic (about 19 percent) and oleic (about 36 percent) [1]. Rendering leaves a solid residue known as cracklings or greaves, used in some dishes and in animal feed [1].

sections.h: How people use tallow for their looks
paras: Two routines overlap. On the dietary side, followers cook with tallow instead of soybean, canola or sunflower oil and pair it with beef, eggs and other animal foods, sometimes as part of a carnivore or 'animal-based' pattern [12][15]. They connect the swap with leaner body composition, steadier energy for training and clearer skin, usually through the idea that avoiding seed oils lowers inflammation. On the topical side, whipped or balm-style tallow products are rubbed on the face, lips, hands and body overnight or after washing, commonly described by sellers and users as suited to dry or sensitive skin.

Tallow also appears in pemmican, the traditional dried-meat and fat mix, which some strength-training forum members make as a portable high-fat food [16], and in everyday cooking posts where lifters mention frying eggs, steak or wings in it [15][17]. In these communities fat choice is treated as one more lever in an appearance routine alongside protein intake and training.

Tallow has been used as a shortening and deep-frying fat and is an ingredient in pemmican. It is the main raw material for soap, producing sodium tallowate, and for centuries it was the standard material for molded candles, with poorer households using cheap tallow dips [1]. It lubricated steam locomotives and ships into the 1950s [1]. Rumours that rifle cartridges were greased with tallow or lard helped spark the Indian Mutiny of 1857 [1]. In 2010 a US Air Force C-17 flew on a blend that included a tallow-derived biofuel [1].

Beef tallow was used for frying at several fast-food chains in the 1980s, and McDonald's, which used a blend of about 93 percent beef tallow and 7 percent cottonseed oil, changed its frying fat in 1990 [1].

sections.h: The seed-oil debate and the political turn
paras: The modern appeal of tallow is tied to the seed-oil avoidance movement. Wikipedia traces popular claims that processed seed oils harm health to around 2018, with a boost in 2020 after carnivore-diet proponent Paul Saladino appeared on the Joe Rogan Experience; physician Cate Shanahan popularised a list of 'hateful eight' oils on a podcast the same year [8]. Critics of seed oils point to industrial processing, hexane extraction residues and the omega-6 fat linoleic acid, which they link to inflammation and chronic disease [8].

Health bodies and researchers cited by Wikipedia, including Harvard-affiliated statements and cancer charities, report that evidence does not support those claims, and that human data show linoleic acid does not raise inflammation markers [8]. Seed-oil scepticism became associated with the political right and with figures such as Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who called seed oils among the least healthy ingredients in food and became US Secretary of Health and Human Services in 2025 [8][11]. Wikipedia reports that the MAHA movement promotes beef tallow as an alternative to seed oils [11].

Restaurants followed. McDonald's had moved away from beef tallow in 1990 after a campaign by businessman Phil Sokolof, who ran full-page newspaper advertisements urging the chain to stop frying in it; the vegetable oils that replaced it were initially hydrogenated and contained trans fats, which the company dropped in 2008 [9]. In February 2025 Steak 'n Shake said it would cook fries in 100 percent beef tallow from 1 March; Kennedy later cited the change as an example of the MAHA agenda, and health experts and scientists criticised the move [10]. Wikipedia also records a 2026 promotion offering a jar of beef tallow cooking oil [10].

Ancestral-diet communities cook with tallow as an alternative to seed oils, which they argue are inflammatory, and some link the switch to leaner physique and clearer skin. A forum member on T Nation describing a diet of beef, sardines, eggs and an animal-based protein powder says simply that they cook with tallow and do not stress about fat intake [15]; another notes that tallow is called dripping in the UK [17]. In these circles dietary fat choice is treated as part of an appearance routine.

Tallow-based balms are applied to the face and body as moisturisers. Proponents say tallow resembles the fats in human skin oil, and reports of smoother skin circulate on social platforms. Human sebum is made up of roughly 41 percent triglycerides, 26 percent wax esters, 16 percent free fatty acids and 12 percent squalene, a composition that includes substances beef fat does not contain [14]. Emollients and occlusives as a class soften skin and limit water loss [4]. The 2025 social-media analysis of tallow skincare claims examined how these claims are presented online [5]. Health-community posts from the period also questioned the practice, such as a Lemmy thread titled as a warning to think twice before putting tallow on the face [6].

A 1965 controlled feeding study of particular saturated fatty acids reported that serum cholesterol responses could largely be predicted by a formula, with discrepancies noted for some fats, including beef tallow and cocoa butter [2]. A 2026 JACC Advances review of trending cardiovascular nutrition controversies placed beef tallow in a group associated with higher LDL cholesterol, alongside ultra-processed foods and some sweeteners, and placed seed oils and seafood in a group linked to cardiovascular benefit [3]. A rodent study reported greater body fat accumulation in rats fed beef tallow than in rats fed safflower oil [7]. These studies concern diet, not appearance.

Guidelines from the American Heart Association, WHO and other bodies advise limiting saturated fat to under about 7 to 10 percent of energy and replacing it with unsaturated fats, and a 2020 Cochrane review reported moderate-quality evidence that reducing saturated fat for at least two years lowers cardiovascular risk [13]. The same Wikipedia summary records dissenting commentary, including a 2010 dietetics conference debate cautioning that replacing saturated fat with refined carbohydrate may not help, and reviews reporting that some individual saturated fatty acids behave differently from others [13]. A 2026 critique of the 2025-2030 US Dietary Guidelines also examined the policy debate on fats [18]. Wikipedia describes tallow-versus-seed-oil frying claims as unscientific [1]; supporters counter that animal fats are traditional foods.

Coverage of tallow has largely been about politics and nutrition rather than appearance. Commentators and health experts criticised the Steak 'n Shake switch and the wider MAHA promotion of tallow, while supporters present it as a return to traditional cooking [10][11]. The carnivore and animal-based diet scene, which includes Shawn Baker, Mikhaila and Jordan Peterson and Paul Saladino, helped popularise animal fats online; neurologist Steven Novella and dietetic associations have called the carnivore diet a fad [12].

On skin, some dermatology researchers have started to document the trend itself. The 2025 analysis of social-media posts examined what benefits and risks tallow skincare content claims [5], and a health-community thread framed the practice as something to think twice about [6]. Acne is linked to sebum, androgens and Cutibacterium acnes [14].

As food, tallow is high in saturated fat and cholesterol, and guideline bodies advise limiting saturated fat [13][3]. Topical use has no published safety data, and moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some people [4].

No human trial has tested beef tallow, eaten or applied topically, for skin or appearance. Related research consists of older feeding studies of saturated fat and serum cholesterol [2], a 2026 review of cardiovascular nutrition controversies [3], rodent diet work [7] and a 2025 cross-sectional analysis of tallow skincare claims on social media [5].

lore.intro: In wellness and looksmaxxing circles, beef tallow is presented as a traditional, seed-oil-free fat for both eating and skin, a trend amplified by influencers, restaurant marketing and political figures [1][10][11].

claims.claim: Tallow is healthier than seed oils for cooking.
claims.believers: Promoters say animal fat is traditional and avoids industrial seed oils and their solvents; the view is promoted by some influencers and by MAHA figures [8][11].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes these claims as unscientific [1], and a 2026 cardiology review links beef tallow with raised LDL cholesterol while associating seed oils with improved cardiovascular outcomes [3]. Health bodies recommend replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat [13].

claims.claim: Tallow on skin works as a moisturiser.
claims.believers: Proponents say tallow resembles human skin oils and report smoother, softer skin online [5].
claims.experts: Moisturisers generally work as occlusives that reduce water loss [4], but human sebum has a different composition from beef fat [14] and no published study tests tallow on skin.

claims.claim: Cooking with tallow improves physique and skin from within.
claims.believers: Ancestral-diet followers say removing seed oils and eating animal fats supports leanness and skin quality [15].
claims.experts: No trial links dietary tallow to appearance; a rat study reported more body fat accumulation on beef tallow than on safflower oil [7].

claims.claim: Seed oils are a main driver of chronic disease.
claims.believers: Seed-oil critics point to processing, hexane and omega-6 intake as causes of inflammation and disease [8].
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites Harvard statements, cancer charities and human data reporting no support for those claims, and reviews linking higher omega-6 levels with lower cardiovascular risk [8].

claims.claim: The McDonald's tallow fries were healthier before 1990.
claims.believers: Supporters of the return-to-tallow view cite the switch to vegetable oils as a step that replaced a natural fat with processed ones [10].
claims.experts: The replacement oils were partially hydrogenated and contained trans fats, later removed [9]; tallow itself remains high in saturated fat [1][13].

claims.claim: Tallow balm suits all skin types, including acne-prone skin.
claims.believers: Sellers and users describe it as gentle and suitable for sensitive skin.
claims.experts: No studies test this; acne is linked to sebum, androgens and C. acnes [14], and a health-forum post urged caution about putting tallow on the face [6].

card.summary: Rendered beef fat used for frying and, lately, as a face moisturiser; popular online, with no trials on its skin or appearance effects.
card.note: High in saturated fat and cholesterol; Wikipedia describes some seed-oil-versus-tallow claims as unscientific.

quick.overview:
Beef tallow is beef fat that has been rendered into a solid. It has long been used for frying, soap and candles, and has recently become popular with ancestral-diet and looksmaxxing communities, both as a cooking fat and as something to rub on the skin.

Its composition is well documented. No published human trial was found testing tallow for skin or appearance, and the claim that it is healthier than seed oils is described by Wikipedia as unscientific.
quick.mechanism: Tallow is almost pure fat, roughly half saturated and 42 percent monounsaturated. As a food it is a calorie-dense frying fat; applied to skin, fats generally act as occlusives that slow water loss. Whether tallow specifically offers skin benefits has not been tested.
quick.risks: As food, tallow is high in saturated fat and cholesterol, and older diet studies found saturated fats raise serum cholesterol. Topical use has no published safety data; moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some people.
